   158→## 4. MUSICA Architecture (from Kyle Shores Presentation)
   159→
   160→MUSICA (Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols) is the core chemistry library that CheMPAS-A integrates.
   161→
   162→### 4.1 Core Design
   163→
   164→**Software requirements (mandatory):**
   165→- Must build as a **standalone library**
   166→- Must have **~80% test coverage**
   167→- Must be **runtime configurable**
   168→
   169→**"Change the data, not the code" philosophy:**
   170→- MUSICA flexibility is provided by an **abstracted data layer**
   171→- Mechanism configuration via **JSON or YAML files** describing the chemical mechanism
   172→- Runtime configuration of the chemistry: "Want a different mechanism? No need to recompile, just change the data"
   173→
   174→**Language support:**
   175→- Using MUSICA from any language is easy
   176→- Provides interfaces for **Python, JavaScript**, and soon **Julia**
   177→- Core implementation in **C++** with Fortran API wrappers
   178→
   179→### 4.2 Build System
   180→
   181→- **CMake** build system
   182→  - Easily builds for any compiler and architecture
   183→  - Fundamental in providing interfaces for Python, JavaScript, and soon Julia
   184→- **C++ standard library** used for core implementation
   185→  - Easier integration with **CUDA** for GPU computing
   186→- **CCPP MUSICA wrapper** targets MUSICA's Fortran layer
   187→  - To maintain **model agnosticism**, CCPP compliance is NOT provided directly with MUSICA, but with a **small shim layer** in the atmospheric physics repository
   188→- **Terminator Chemistry** test proves MICM and TUV-x work in CAM-SIMA
   189→
   190→### 4.3 MPAS-A Integration Status
   191→
   192→**Active pull requests:**
   193→- `github.com/MPAS-Dev/MPAS-Model/pull/1309` -- initial build support
   194→- `github.com/MPAS-Dev/MPAS-Model/pull/1360` -- continued integration
   195→- `github.com/MPAS-Dev/MPAS-Model/pull/1376` -- further integration work
   196→
   197→**Current approach:**
   198→- Initial PRs add build support and start with **hard-coded species** until MPAS can support runtime constituents
   199→- MICM will be integrated first, followed shortly by TUV-x
   200→- **Target: Potentially completed by Summer 2026**
   201→
   202→### 4.4 QUACS Scripting Vision
   203→
   204→QUACS (Quick Updates for Atmospheric Chemistry Simulations) extends CheMPAS-A with a scripting layer:
   205→
   206→**Game-engine analogy:**
   207→- Scripting languages are used extensively in the software world: game engines (Unity, Godot), 3D modeling (Blender, Maya), parametric modelling (CAD), physics modeling (MuJoCo, CARLA, Gazebo)
   208→- "Why not also MPAS and other weather models?"
   209→
   210→**Benefits:**
   211→- May be faster to try out many things
   212→- Lower barrier to entry -- most students are more likely to be familiar with scripting languages
   213→- Creates a scripting language to support atmospheric chemistry simulations

   217→## 5. CATChem Architecture (from CATChem Restructure Status)
   218→
   219→CATChem (Community Atmospheric chemistry Treatment in Chemistry) is the NOAA/UFS chemistry framework being generalized. This is directly relevant to CheMPAS-A as a parallel effort with shared goals.
   220→
   221→### 5.1 Process-Based Design
   222→
   223→Each CATChem process follows a standardized three-phase lifecycle:
   224→
   225→**Initialize phase (`CCPr_<process>_mod.F90`):**
   226→- Uses the `ConfigState` to set options (defined in the YAML file)
   227→- Allocates any arrays needed for the process
   228→
   229→**Run phase:**
   230→- Looks at the process configuration and chooses the appropriate "scheme"
   231→- All schemes follow the naming convention `CCPr_scheme_<name>_mod.F90`
   232→- Adds to `DiagState`, `EmisState`, and `ChemState` where appropriate based on configuration
   233→- Standardized Met variables come from `MetState`
   234→- Process-specific variables available for all schemes
   235→- Scheme-specific options for fine-grained control
   236→
   237→**Finalize phase:**
   238→- Deallocate any local arrays
   239→
   240→CATChem processes are defined as a "specific physical/chemical process unique to chemical modeling." Examples include dust emission, photolysis, dry deposition, etc. Each process has a "driver" found in the `src/process` directory.
   241→
   242→### 5.2 State Interfaces
   243→
   244→CATChem defines four core state objects for uniform data exchange:
   245→
   246→| State Object | Description |
   247→|---|---|
   248→| **`ConfigState`** | Runtime configuration settings loaded from YAML; used during process initialization to set options |
   249→| **`DiagState`** | Diagnostic state for output and monitoring; processes add diagnostics during their Run phase |
   250→| **`EmisState`** | Emission state containing emission sectors, categories, emitted species with mapping, scaling, plume rise options |
   251→| **`ChemState`** | Chemical state housing `ChemStateType` with species names, species containers; allows quick indexing for host models and internal processes; **defined at runtime through a YAML file** |
   252→
   253→**ChemState detail -- species properties include:**
   254→- `short_name`, `long_name`, `description`
   255→- Boolean flags: `is_gas`, `is_aerosol`, `is_tracer`, `is_advected`, `is_drydep`, `is_photolysis`, `is_dust`, `is_seasalt`
   256→- Physical properties: `mw_g` (molecular weight), `density`, `radius`, `lower_radius`, `upper_radius`, `viscosity`
   257→
   258→**EmisState detail -- hierarchical structure:**
   259→- All Emission sectors (contains array of emission "categories")
   260→- Each Emission Category contains an array of emitted species
   261→- Each Emitted Species has: `long_name`, `scale` (linear scaling array), `map` (mapping to chemical species array), `plumerise_opt` (default 0 for none), `emislayer` (if not at surface)
   262→- Plume rise options being added: Sofiev, Briggs, and a simple height-weighted thickness similar to HEMCO options
   263→
   264→**Data flow:** Host model provides `MetState` -> CATChem processes read `ConfigState` for options -> processes operate on `ChemState`/`EmisState` -> processes write to `DiagState`
   265→
   266→### 5.3 Scheme Selection
   267→
   268→CATChem uses a **"flat" scheme selection** approach from configuration:
   269→
   270→- Specific schemes are added as "flat" processes
   271→- These could be from an **external submodule** (such as GOCART) or a process included directly into CATChem
   272→- The process Run phase checks configuration and selects the appropriate scheme
   273→- Only activated processes are executed ("Only do process if activated")
   274→- "Scheme" option is set during the Init phase based on YAML configuration
   275→
   276→**Example flow in the Run phase:**
   277→1. Check if process is activated
   278→2. Read scheme option (set during Init)
   279→3. Pass standardized Met variables from `MetState`
   280→4. Execute scheme-specific code
   281→5. Update `DiagState`, `EmisState`, and `ChemState`
   282→
   283→### 5.4 External Submodules
   284→
   285→- **GOCART2G** is added as a submodule in a new "external" folder
   286→- Only the "Process_Library" is able to interface and be built within CATChem
   287→- Specific processes are linked into CATChem as options (first: DryDeposition via `CCPr_drydep`)
   288→- Repository: `https://github.com/bbakernoaa/CATChem/tree/feature/catchem_begins`
   289→- Documentation from the beginning: `https://bbakernoaa.github.io/CATChem/index.html`
   290→
   291→**Additional infrastructure:**
   292→- `src/core/constants.F90` -- global constants (gravity, specific heat, etc.)
   293→- `src/core/precision_mod.F90` -- precision and missing values used throughout CATChem
   294→- CATChem API provides high-level interface to the host model (usable via NUOPC, FMS, CCPP wrapper, or direct CCPP physics call)
   295→
   296→**Next steps (at time of presentation):**
   297→- Add new processes: MEGAN, Canopy-App, and more
   298→- Add additional linkages to GOCART2G library
   299→- Integrate Jian's AM4 work, Lori's GHG work
   300→- Integrate MICM

   187→## D. Species Mapping
   188→
   189→### D.1 The Mapping Problem
   190→
   191→Each emission inventory uses different species names and lumping. Each chemical mechanism defines different surrogate species. A configurable mapping layer (YAML/JSON) must translate between them. CATChem's `EmisState` hierarchy (sector -> category -> emitted species -> mapped chemical species, with scaling and plume rise options) is the most detailed reference.
   192→
   193→> **Source:** `phase1-technical-architect.md` line 200
   194→
   195→### D.2 CATChem Emission Mapping Pattern
   196→
   197→CATChem defines a sophisticated emission mapping system where each emitted species can map to one or more chemical species with scaling factors, plume rise options, and emission layer specifications — all via YAML.
   198→
   199→CATChem state objects: `EmisState` — Hierarchical emission structure: sectors -> categories -> emitted species -> mapped chemical species, with scaling arrays and plume rise options.
   200→
   201→> **Source:** `phase1-cutting-edge.md` lines 46, 66 (CATChem EmisState description); `phase1_cutting_edge.md` lines 46-47

   204→
   205→**Species-to-slot mapping flow:**
   206→```
   207→MICM JSON ──(1)──> CheMPAS-A YAML ──(3)──> MPAS Registry Slots
   208→(species list)     (emissions_mapping:       (chem_tracer(1,:,:)
   209→                     CAMS_NO → NO             chem_tracer(2,:,:)
   210→                     CAMS_NO2 → NO2)          ...)
   211→```
   212→
   213→**CheMPAS-A YAML emissions section:**
   214→```yaml
   215→emissions:
   216→  sectors: [anthro, fire, bio]
   217→  mapping:
   218→    inventory_NO  → MICM_NO
   219→    inventory_NO2 → MICM_NO2
   220→```
   221→
   222→> **Source:** `phase2_technical_architect.md` lines 624-631; `phase2_engineering_lead.md` lines 226-231
   223→
   224→**Cutting Edge YAML example:**
   225→```yaml
   226→chempas:
   227→  processes:
   228→    emissions:
   229→      enabled: true
   230→      config_file: "emissions/emissions.yaml"
   231→```
   232→
   233→> **Source:** `phase2_cutting_edge.md` lines 609-611

   235→**Engineering Lead emissions_mapping YAML:**

   238→  CAMS_NO → NO

## Overview

The Model Independent Chemistry Module (MICM) is being built to allow chemistry schemes (including calculation of photolysis rates and rate constants, and solving the chemistry ODEs) to be maintained in one place yet applied in any atmosphere model.

## Custom Rate Parameters

The MICM module has been developed to include a variety of ways in calculating reaction rate constants (including heterogeneous reactions) and a fast, accurate solver for integrating the differential equations that represent the chemistry. MICM supports different rate constant parameterizations, such as the Arrhenius equation, which allows customization of reaction rate parameters (pre-exponential factor, temperature dependence, etc.).

## Emissions Handling

MICM enables community users to implement their own system of chemical reactions (via the Chemistry Cafe) and other input parameters, including surface emission and deposition rates. Additionally, an emissions tool was built to regrid emission inventories from the latitude-longitude and point source emissions datasets onto the unstructured model grid mesh of CAM Spectral Element with regional refinement, and this emissions tool is being applied to both anthropogenic and fire emissions.

## Chemistry Solver Interface

At the heart of MUSICA is the standalone Model Independent Chemistry Model (MICM) that satisfies the requirements of the Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) and that can be connected to any CCPP compliant atmosphere model. The system supports multiple solver options and is designed with a flexible architecture for handling various chemical mechanisms.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about CAM-chem HEMCO emissions regridding runtime offline SE grid CESM:

## Overview

HEMCO-CESM is the official interface coupling the Harmonized Emissions Component (HEMCO) to the Community Earth System Model version 2 (CESM2) via the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM).

## Regridding Capabilities

HEMCO in CESM runs on its own separate grid and MPI decomposition and regrids its computed data to the CAM grid, which is important for handling different model resolutions. During initialization, the HEMCO–CESM Model Interface Layer reads the ESMF mesh file that describes the grid used by CAM and uses ESMF online re-gridding to re-grid data between HEMCO and CAM. By using ESMF re-gridding capabilities, HEMCO is capable of operating independently of the grid used by the model, as long as the model grid description is provided to HEMCO using an ESMF mesh file.

## Runtime Configuration

HEMCO is configured as a runtime option using use_hemco = .true. in the physics control namelist to control HEMCO routine at runtime. It works with CESM 2.2 and above with any grid, tested with 1.9x2.5, 0.9x1.25, ne30np4, ne0np4.KORUS03.ne30x16.

## Spectral Element (SE) Grid Support

New emission regridding tools are available. The system supports various grid types including the spectral element grid commonly used in CAM.

# Chemistry Integration in CAM-SIMA

Based on the webpage content provided, here's what the documentation reveals:

## Model Independent Chemistry Module (MICM)

NCAR is developing MICM as a portable infrastructure for chemistry schemes. The module is designed as "model independent" to enable chemistry calculations to be "maintained in one place yet applied in any atmosphere model," covering photolysis rates, rate constants, and ODE solving.

## MUSICA Integration Approach

MUSICA v0 demonstrates the integration strategy:

**Emissions Handling:**
An emissions tool was specifically created to "regrid emission inventories from the latitude-longitude and point source emissions datasets onto the unstructured model grid mesh." This tool processes both anthropogenic and fire emissions, adapting them to CAM's Spectral Element grid with regional refinement capabilities.

**Implementation Details:**
The current configuration uses "a grid mesh with global horizontal grid spacing of 1˚ that refines to 0.125˚ (~14km) over the conterminous U.S." This demonstrates how emissions data is transformed to match the host model's grid structure before chemistry calculations.

## Key Limitation

The provided content describes the emissions infrastructure and MICM framework but does not explicitly detail the specific mechanisms for passing emissions to the chemistry solver or the complete technical workflow between the emissions tool and MICM execution.

## Research Findings: MIEM and the Emissions Data Flow Across MPAS-GOCART2G, CheMPAS, and MUSICA

### 1. MPAS-GOCART2G Emissions Pipeline: Complete Chain from Raw Inventory to Chemical Tendency

The current MPAS-GOCART2G emissions pipeline operates in a **two-stage process** analogous to WRF-Chem's `real.exe`/`wrf.exe` split:

**Offline Preprocessing (UPTEMPO):**
Raw emission inventories (CAMS anthropogenic on 0.1x0.1 degree lat-lon, FINN fire text files, CAMS biogenic) are regridded to the MPAS unstructured Voronoi mesh using ESMF conservative remapping. UPTEMPO outputs NetCDF files with dimensions `(nCells, Time)` in units of `kg m^-2 s^-1`.

**Stage 1 -- `init_atmosphere` (Staging):**
The `mpas_chemistry_init_gocart2G_emissions.F90` module contains per-species subroutines (e.g., `init_anth_emissions_bc`) that:
1. Read before/after timestep emission files via the MPAS stream manager
2. Linearly interpolate to the current model time
3. Write the result into `init_chems_emissions.nc`

**Stage 2 -- `atmosphere` (Runtime):**
1. `mpas_chemistry_gocart2G_emissions_init` extracts emissions from the `anth_emissions` pool into the `emis_gocart2G` derived type -- a massive structure with ~60+ individually named pointer arrays (one per species-sector combination like `bc_antebc1`, `oc_biomass`, `su_shipso2`, etc.)
2. The `gocart2G_timetracker` in the manager module controls when emission updates occur (configurable intervals per sector)
3. `GOCART2G_Process.F90` converts emission fluxes to mixing ratio tendencies. For carbonaceous aerosols, `CAEmissions` handles the conversion; for sulfate, `SulfateDistributeEmissions` does the same. Mode splitting happens at emission time (e.g., BC: 80% hydrophobic, 20% hydrophilic)
4. Tendencies are integrated into the dynamics step

The interface layer between MPAS and GOCART2G handles mapping between MPAS's 1-D mesh `(k,i)` and the 2-D/3-D `(i,j,k)` structure that GOCART2G expects (originally written for regular grids).

**Key files in MPAS-GOCART2G:**
- `src/core_atmosphere/chemistry/mpas_chemistry_gocart2G_emissions.F90` -- the `emis_gocart2G` type and allocation
- `src/core_atmosphere/chemistry/mpas_chemistry_gocart2G_emissions_init.F90` -- init-stage reading
- `src/core_atmosphere/chemistry/Registry_gocart2G_emissions.xml` -- all ~50+ emission variables defined individually
- `src/core_atmosphere/chemistry/GOCART2G_Process.F90` -- flux-to-tendency conversion

### 2. Why UPTEMPO Exists

UPTEMPO exists because MPAS cannot do mass-conservative emission regridding at runtime, and its `init_atmosphere` core is not designed for this purpose. The specific reasons:

**What MPAS `init_atmosphere` can do:** Interpolate meteorological initial conditions from regular grids (GFS, ERA5) to the Voronoi mesh, and process static geographical fields. It uses its own interpolation routines.

**What MPAS cannot do at runtime that UPTEMPO does offline:**

1. **ESMF conservative regridding on unstructured meshes.** MPAS's native interpolation is bilinear, not conservative. For emissions, mass conservation is critical -- you cannot lose or create mass during regridding. UPTEMPO uses `esmpy` with `Conserve` method, which requires precomputed weight files between source and destination grids.

2. **Format and convention translation.** Raw inventories vary enormously: CAMS is on 0.1x0.1 degree lat-lon with sector-specific variables; FINN comes as text files with point-source lat/lon/area. UPTEMPO normalizes all of these into the `(nCells, Time)` layout that MPAS expects, with species renamed to GOCART2G conventions (e.g., FINN `BC` becomes `bc_biob_modis`).

3. **Temporal disaggregation.** UPTEMPO applies climatological diurnal profiles to FINN daily data, creating hourly emissions files with the `lt_fac` weighting array.

4. **Weight file reuse.** The ESMF weight file is expensive to compute but is grid-pair-specific. UPTEMPO computes it once and reuses it for all species/sectors. At runtime, MPAS would need to compute or load these weights, adding complexity and memory overhead.

5. **Grid description file generation.** UPTEMPO requires an ESMF-compliant SCRIP file for the MPAS mesh (created by `mpas2esmf`). This is a preprocessing step that MPAS itself does not produce.

### 3. What MIEM Replaces in GOCART-2G

MIEM replaces the **entire offline emissions reading and processing pipeline** in GOCART2G, but it does NOT replace online emissions (dust, sea-salt) or the GOCART2G aerosol chemistry itself.

**Specifically, MIEM replaces:**

| GOCART2G Component | What It Does | MIEM Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `emis_gocart2G` type (60+ named pointers) | Holds emission fluxes per species-sector | `EmisState` with flat arrays indexed by aggregated species |
| Per-species `init_anth_emissions_*` subroutines | Read NetCDF, temporal interpolation | `SourceOffline::Update()` with `TemporalInterpolator` |
| `Registry_gocart2G_emissions.xml` (50+ variable definitions) | Compile-time variable definitions | YAML configuration at runtime |
| Hardcoded species naming in `GOCART2G_Process.F90` | `CAEmissions`, `SulfateDistributeEmissions` | `SpeciesMap::Apply()` with configurable inventory-to-mechanism mapping |
| Hardcoded VOC factors (`voc_AnthroFactor = 0.069`) | Species speciation constants in Fortran | YAML scaling factors in `SpeciesMapping` |
| `FluxToMixingRatio` logic in `GOCART2G_Process.F90` | `flux / (rho * dz)` conversion | `FluxConverter::Convert()` |

**What MIEM does NOT replace:**
- Online dust emissions (Ginoux parameterization) -- stays in GOCART2G or future `chempas_emissions_dust`
- Online sea-salt emissions (Gong parameterization) -- same
- DMS ocean emissions -- same
- The GOCART2G aerosol chemistry itself (hydrophobic/hydrophilic conversion, settling, wet/dry deposition)
- The GOCART2G-to-MPAS interface layer (grid mapping)

**The key architectural shift:** GOCART2G has ~60 individually named emission pointer variables hardcoded in Fortran, each requiring a Registry XML entry, a stream definition, and per-species init/read code. MIEM replaces this with a single YAML-driven pipeline where adding a new species requires only editing configuration, not Fortran source.

### 4. MIEM to MICM Interface: How Emissions Flow to the Chemistry Solver

The full chain operates as follows. This is based on the design documents and the current MIEM code:

**Step 1 -- Species Discovery (before construction):**
```
Host model calls: MIEM::QuerySpecies(config_path)
  -> Reads YAML, creates sources via factory
  -> Each source returns mechanism species names from its SpeciesMap
  -> Returns aggregated list of mechanism species (e.g., ["NO", "NO2", "SO2", ...])
```

**Step 2 -- Host Index Resolution (after construction):**
```
Host model calls: miem.ResolveHostIndices(host_species_list, indices)
  -> host_species_list comes from MICM's species list (or the Constituent Manager)
  -> indices[i] = position of emission species i in the host's tracer array
  -> -1 means "no match" (emission species not in mechanism)
```
This is where MIEM species get mapped to MICM species. The host model (CheMPAS Fortran layer) provides its species list, which comes from MICM's JSON mechanism configuration.

**Step 3 -- Run (each timestep):**
```
Host calls: EmisState = miem.Run(time, air_density, layer_thickness, n_elements)
  -> Each SourceOffline reads/interpolates NetCDF data
  -> SpeciesMap::Apply() translates inventory names to mechanism names with scaling
  -> FluxConverter::Convert() produces tendency array (kg/kg/s)
  -> EmisState returned with:
      - surface_flux[n_species * n_cells] in kg/m2/s
      - tendency[n_species * n_vert_levels * n_cells] in kg/kg/s
      - emis_to_chem_idx[n_species] mapping to host chemistry indices
```

**Step 4 -- Host injection into MICM (the handoff):**
The host model (CheMPAS Fortran driver) receives the `emis_state_t` and must:
1. Loop over emission species
2. Use `emis_to_chem_idx` to find the corresponding slot in the chemistry state
3. Add the tendency to the species concentration before calling MICM

**MICM does NOT have a dedicated "emissions" mechanism.** Instead, MICM provides `UserDefinedRateConstant` which accepts externally set rate parameters. For emissions, there are two integration patterns:

**Pattern A (Direct tendency injection):** The host adds `tendency * dt` directly to species concentrations in the `ChemState` before calling `MICM::Solve()`. This is the simpler approach and matches the operator-splitting design (`L_emissions(dt) * L_chemistry(dt) * C(t)`).

**Pattern B (Emission as pseudo-reaction via UserDefinedRateConstant):** Emissions can be expressed as zero-order reactions: `-> Species` with a user-defined rate constant set to the emission rate (molecules/cm3/s or equivalent). MICM's `UserDefinedRateConstant` takes a label and a scaling factor, and the host sets the custom parameter value each timestep. This approach integrates emissions within the chemistry solve, reducing operator splitting error.

The design documents indicate **Pattern A for v1** (Lie splitting: emissions before chemistry) and potentially Pattern B for later versions.

**Where species mapping happens:** At `ResolveHostIndices()` time. The MIEM `SpeciesMap` translates inventory names (e.g., `CAMS_NO`) to mechanism names (e.g., `NO`). The host then maps mechanism names to MICM's internal species indices. The `emis_to_chem_idx` array in `EmisState` carries this mapping at runtime.

### 5. Runtime vs. Offline Regridding Trade-offs

| Factor | Offline (UPTEMPO) | Runtime (HEMCO/ESMF) |
|---|---|---|
| **Computational cost** | One-time preprocessing cost; zero runtime cost | Weight computation or loading each run; regridding each emission update |
| **Memory** | Only model-grid data in memory at runtime | Source grid + target grid + weight matrix in memory simultaneously |
| **File I/O** | Reads pre-regridded files (small, fast reads) | Reads native-grid files (potentially much larger: 0.1 degree global = 3600x1800 per species per time) |
| **Mass conservation** | ESMF conservative guaranteed; can be verified offline | Same algorithms, but harder to verify at scale |
| **Preprocessing complexity** | Requires UPTEMPO workflow, conda environment, weight files, SCRIP grids | No preprocessing; "just run" |
| **Grid flexibility** | Must re-run UPTEMPO for every new mesh | Automatically adapts to any mesh at runtime |
| **Variable-resolution meshes** | Works fine (ESMF handles unstructured) | Works fine but weight computation is expensive for high-res refinement regions |
| **Disk storage** | N copies of emissions (one per resolution) | One copy of native-grid emissions |
| **Reproducibility** | Deterministic (same preprocessed files) | May vary with decomposition if parallel regridding is used |
| **User burden** | High: multiple scripts, config files, manual steps | Low: point at raw inventory, run model |

**Why MPAS chose offline regridding:** MPAS's unstructured Voronoi mesh makes runtime regridding particularly expensive. The irregular cell geometry means ESMF weight computation is O(N*M) where N and M are source and target cells, and for a 0.1-degree global inventory onto a 60km MPAS mesh, that is ~6.5M source cells to 164K target cells. Computing this at every model start adds significant overhead. UPTEMPO precomputes the weights once per grid pair.

### 6. How CAM-chem/CAM-SIMA Handles Emissions

CAM-chem and CAM-SIMA take a fundamentally different approach from MPAS-GOCART2G:

**CAM-chem (current/legacy):**
- Emissions are preprocessed offline using tools like `emissions_to_SE.py` that regrid lat-lon inventories to the Spectral Element (SE) grid
- The regridded files are read at runtime via CAM's `shr_infnan` I/O infrastructure
- Species mapping is handled through `chem_surfvals` and hardcoded in the chemistry preprocessor

**CAM-SIMA with HEMCO (emerging):**
- [HEMCO_CESM](https://github.com/ESCOMP/HEMCO_CESM) provides **runtime regridding** using ESMF
- HEMCO runs on its own separate grid and MPI decomposition
- It reads native-grid inventories and regrids to the CAM grid using ESMF online remapping
- Configuration is entirely runtime via text-based HEMCO configuration files (no recompilation)
- Species scaling, masking, temporal disaggregation, and sector selection all happen at runtime
- This was [integrated into CESM via PR #560](https://github.com/ESCOMP/CAM/pull/560) for CAM 6.3.118+

**Comparison to MPAS approach:**

| Aspect | MPAS-GOCART2G | CAM-chem | CAM-SIMA/HEMCO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regridding | Offline (UPTEMPO) | Offline (SE tools) | Runtime (ESMF) |
| Configuration | Hardcoded Fortran + Registry XML | Hardcoded preprocessor | Runtime text config |
| Adding species | Edit Fortran + XML + UPTEMPO scripts | Edit preprocessor + namelist | Edit HEMCO config file |
| Grid types | Unstructured Voronoi | Spectral Element, FV | Any (ESMF mesh) |
| Preprocessing burden | High (UPTEMPO + conda) | Moderate (SE regridding) | None |

CAM-SIMA's HEMCO approach is the direction the community is moving. The CheMPAS design exploration evaluated HEMCO for MPAS but flagged its compatibility with unstructured grids as unvalidated (Design Question #9 in the synthesis). The resolution was: evaluate HEMCO's MPAS compatibility during Phase A; adopt if viable, otherwise modernize UPTEMPO.

### 7. CheMPAS Design Context from NCAR/chempas-emissions-design

The [NCAR/chempas-emissions-design](https://github.com/NCAR/chempas-emissions-design) repository contains the complete design exploration and v1 implementation plan for how MIEM (originally designed as Fortran modules) fits into CheMPAS-A.

**Key findings from the design repository:**

The design was produced through a multi-agent exploration (5 specialist agents across 4 phases) that produced 14 consensus decisions. For emissions specifically:

1. **v1 scope:** MICM + TUV-x + offline emissions only (anthropogenic, prescribed biogenic, prescribed fires). Target: August 2026.

2. **MIEM's role:** MIEM is the C++ implementation of what the design exploration called `chempas_emissions_offline` -- the offline emission reader module. The design originally specified Fortran source modules (`chempas_emis_state.F90`, `chempas_emissions_offline.F90`, `chempas_emis_species_map.F90`), but MIEM implements this as C++ core with Fortran bindings via the MUSICA three-layer pattern (C++ -> C API -> Fortran `iso_c_binding`).

3. **Three architectural seams:**
   - **Seam 1 (Host/Chemistry):** Typed state objects (EmisState, ChemState, MetState) as the data contract between MPAS pools and the chemistry layer
   - **Seam 2 (Chemistry/Processes):** Abstract process interface with init/run/finalize lifecycle
   - **Seam 3 (CheMPAS-A/MUSICA):** Unit conversion (kg/kg to mol/m3), precision promotion (single to double), copy-in/copy-out

4. **Process ordering constraint:** Emissions MUST execute before chemistry. The pipeline is: `emissions_offline -> photolysis (TUV-x) -> gas_chemistry (MICM)`.

5. **Risk R9 was prescient:** "Emission pipeline complexity underestimated" -- all five design agents flagged emissions as under-specified and needing dedicated design attention. MIEM is the response to that risk.

6. **10 design gaps resolved:** Including file format spec (CF-compliant NetCDF3, `(Time, nCells)`, `emi_<SPECIES>` naming, `kg m-2 s-1`), temporal interpolation (linear for monthly, step for daily/hourly), vertical distribution (surface-only for v1), and non-1:1 species mapping (VOC speciation via multi-target mapping with scaling factors).

The `emissions-extraction` branch of the design repo contains the complete consolidated context, including Fortran prototypes and test specifications (10 files total) that informed MIEM's C++ implementation.

---

**Sources:**

- [PACE-DAAQ/MPAS-GOCART2G](https://github.com/PACE-DAAQ/MPAS-GOCART2G) -- MPAS-GOCART2G source code
- [PACE-DAAQ/UPTEMPO](https://github.com/PACE-DAAQ/UPTEMPO) -- Unified Processing Tool for Emissions in MPAS-A GOCART
- [NCAR/chempas-emissions-design](https://github.com/NCAR/chempas-emissions-design) -- CheMPAS-A v1 emissions architecture
- [NCAR/micm](https://github.com/NCAR/micm) -- Model Independent Chemistry Module
- [NCAR/musica](https://github.com/NCAR/musica) -- Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry Modeling
- [ESCOMP/HEMCO_CESM](https://github.com/ESCOMP/HEMCO_CESM) -- HEMCO integration in CESM
- [HEMCO in CAM PR #560](https://github.com/ESCOMP/CAM/pull/560) -- CAM HEMCO integration pull request
- [CAM-SIMA Chemistry](https://sima.ucar.edu/applications/v0/chemistry) -- MUSICA v0 chemistry documentation
- [HEMCO 3.0 paper (Lin et al., 2021 GMD)](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/14/5487/2021/) -- HEMCO reference publication

| Per-species `init_anth_emissions_*` subroutines | Read NetCDF, temporal interpolation | `SourceOffline::Update()` with `TemporalInterpolator` |
| `Registry_gocart2G_emissions.xml` (50+ variable definitions) | Compile-time variable definitions | YAML configuration at runtime |
| Hardcoded species naming in `GOCART2G_Process.F90` | `CAEmissions`, `SulfateDistributeEmissions` | `SpeciesMap::Apply()` with configurable inventory-to-mechanism mapping |
| Hardcoded VOC factors (`voc_AnthroFactor = 0.069`) | Species speciation constants in Fortran | YAML scaling factors in `SpeciesMapping` |
| `FluxToMixingRatio` logic in `GOCART2G_Process.F90` | `flux / (rho * dz)` conversion | `FluxConverter::Convert()` |

**What MIEM does NOT replace:**
- Online dust emissions (Ginoux parameterization) -- stays in GOCART2G or future `chempas_emissions_dust`
- Online sea-salt emissions (Gong parameterization) -- same
- DMS ocean emissions -- same
- The GOCART2G aerosol chemistry itself (hydrophobic/hydrophilic conversion, settling, wet/dry deposition)
- The GOCART2G-to-MPAS interface layer (grid mapping)

**The key architectural shift:** GOCART2G has ~60 individually named emission pointer variables hardcoded in Fortran, each requiring a Registry XML entry, a stream definition, and per-species init/read code. MIEM replaces this with a single YAML-driven pipeline where adding a new species requires only editing configuration, not Fortran source.

### 4. MIEM to MICM Interface: How Emissions Flow to the Chemistry Solver

The full chain operates as follows. This is based on the design documents and the current MIEM code:

**Step 1 -- Species Discovery (before construction):**
```
Host model calls: MIEM::QuerySpecies(config_path)
  -> Reads YAML, creates sources via factory
  -> Each source returns mechanism species names from its SpeciesMap
  -> Returns aggregated list of mechanism species (e.g., ["NO", "NO2", "SO2", ...])
```

**Step 2 -- Host Index Resolution (after construction):**
```
Host model calls: miem.ResolveHostIndices(host_species_list, indices)
  -> host_species_list comes from MICM's species list (or the Constituent Manager)
  -> indices[i] = position of emission species i in the host's tracer array
  -> -1 means "no match" (emission species not in mechanism)
```
This is where MIEM species get mapped to MICM species. The host model (CheMPAS Fortran layer) provides its species list, which comes from MICM's JSON mechanism configuration.

**Step 3 -- Run (each timestep):**
```
Host calls: EmisState = miem.Run(time, air_density, layer_thickness, n_elements)
  -> Each SourceOffline reads/interpolates NetCDF data
  -> SpeciesMap::Apply() translates inventory names to mechanism names with scaling
  -> FluxConverter::Convert() produces tendency array (kg/kg/s)
  -> EmisState returned with:
      - surface_flux[n_species * n_cells] in kg/m2/s
      - tendency[n_species * n_vert_levels * n_cells] in kg/kg/s
      - emis_to_chem_idx[n_species] mapping to host chemistry indices
```

**Step 4 -- Host injection into MICM (the handoff):**
The host model (CheMPAS Fortran driver) receives the `emis_state_t` and must:
1. Loop over emission species
2. Use `emis_to_chem_idx` to find the corresponding slot in the chemistry state
3. Add the tendency to the species concentration before calling MICM

**MICM does NOT have a dedicated "emissions" mechanism.** Instead, MICM provides `UserDefinedRateConstant` which accepts externally set rate parameters. For emissions, there are two integration patterns:

**Pattern A (Direct tendency injection):** The host adds `tendency * dt` directly to species concentrations in the `ChemState` before calling `MICM::Solve()`. This is the simpler approach and matches the operator-splitting design (`L_emissions(dt) * L_chemistry(dt) * C(t)`).

**Pattern B (Emission as pseudo-reaction via UserDefinedRateConstant):** Emissions can be expressed as zero-order reactions: `-> Species` with a user-defined rate constant set to the emission rate (molecules/cm3/s or equivalent). MICM's `UserDefinedRateConstant` takes a label and a scaling factor, and the host sets the custom parameter value each timestep. This approach integrates emissions within the chemistry solve, reducing operator splitting error.

The design documents indicate **Pattern A for v1** (Lie splitting: emissions before chemistry) and potentially Pattern B for later versions.

**Where species mapping happens:** At `ResolveHostIndices()` time. The MIEM `SpeciesMap` translates inventory names (e.g., `CAMS_NO`) to mechanism names (e.g., `NO`). The host then maps mechanism names to MICM's internal species indices. The `emis_to_chem_idx` array in `EmisState` carries this mapping at runtime.

### 5. Runtime vs. Offline Regridding Trade-offs

| Factor | Offline (UPTEMPO) | Runtime (HEMCO/ESMF) |
|---|---|---|
| **Computational cost** | One-time preprocessing cost; zero runtime cost | Weight computation or loading each run; regridding each emission update |
| **Memory** | Only model-grid data in memory at runtime | Source grid + target grid + weight matrix in memory simultaneously |
| **File I/O** | Reads pre-regridded files (small, fast reads) | Reads native-grid files (potentially much larger: 0.1 degree global = 3600x1800 per species per time) |
| **Mass conservation** | ESMF conservative guaranteed; can be verified offline | Same algorithms, but harder to verify at scale |
| **Preprocessing complexity** | Requires UPTEMPO workflow, conda environment, weight files, SCRIP grids | No preprocessing; "just run" |
| **Grid flexibility** | Must re-run UPTEMPO for every new mesh | Automatically adapts to any mesh at runtime |
| **Variable-resolution meshes** | Works fine (ESMF handles unstructured) | Works fine but weight computation is expensive for high-res refinement regions |
| **Disk storage** | N copies of emissions (one per resolution) | One copy of native-grid emissions |
| **Reproducibility** | Deterministic (same preprocessed files) | May vary with decomposition if parallel regridding is used |
| **User burden** | High: multiple scripts, config files, manual steps | Low: point at raw inventory, run model |

**Why MPAS chose offline regridding:** MPAS's unstructured Voronoi mesh makes runtime regridding particularly expensive. The irregular cell geometry means ESMF weight computation is O(N*M) where N and M are source and target cells, and for a 0.1-degree global inventory onto a 60km MPAS mesh, that is ~6.5M source cells to 164K target cells. Computing this at every model start adds significant overhead. UPTEMPO precomputes the weights once per grid pair.

### 6. How CAM-chem/CAM-SIMA Handles Emissions

CAM-chem and CAM-SIMA take a fundamentally different approach from MPAS-GOCART2G:

**CAM-chem (current/legacy):**
- Emissions are preprocessed offline using tools like `emissions_to_SE.py` that regrid lat-lon inventories to the Spectral Element (SE) grid
- The regridded files are read at runtime via CAM's `shr_infnan` I/O infrastructure
- Species mapping is handled through `chem_surfvals` and hardcoded in the chemistry preprocessor

**CAM-SIMA with HEMCO (emerging):**
- [HEMCO_CESM](https://github.com/ESCOMP/HEMCO_CESM) provides **runtime regridding** using ESMF
- HEMCO runs on its own separate grid and MPI decomposition
- It reads native-grid inventories and regrids to the CAM grid using ESMF online remapping
- Configuration is entirely runtime via text-based HEMCO configuration files (no recompilation)
- Species scaling, masking, temporal disaggregation, and sector selection all happen at runtime
- This was [integrated into CESM via PR #560](https://github.com/ESCOMP/CAM/pull/560) for CAM 6.3.118+

**Comparison to MPAS approach:**

| Aspect | MPAS-GOCART2G | CAM-chem | CAM-SIMA/HEMCO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regridding | Offline (UPTEMPO) | Offline (SE tools) | Runtime (ESMF) |
| Configuration | Hardcoded Fortran + Registry XML | Hardcoded preprocessor | Runtime text config |
| Adding species | Edit Fortran + XML + UPTEMPO scripts | Edit preprocessor + namelist | Edit HEMCO config file |
| Grid types | Unstructured Voronoi | Spectral Element, FV | Any (ESMF mesh) |
| Preprocessing burden | High (UPTEMPO + conda) | Moderate (SE regridding) | None |

CAM-SIMA's HEMCO approach is the direction the community is moving. The CheMPAS design exploration evaluated HEMCO for MPAS but flagged its compatibility with unstructured grids as unvalidated (Design Question #9 in the synthesis). The resolution was: evaluate HEMCO's MPAS compatibility during Phase A; adopt if viable, otherwise modernize UPTEMPO.

### 7. CheMPAS Design Context from NCAR/chempas-emissions-design

The [NCAR/chempas-emissions-design](https://github.com/NCAR/chempas-emissions-design) repository contains the complete design exploration and v1 implementation plan for how MIEM (originally designed as Fortran modules) fits into CheMPAS-A.

**Key findings from the design repository:**

The design was produced through a multi-agent exploration (5 specialist agents across 4 phases) that produced 14 consensus decisions. For emissions specifically:

1. **v1 scope:** MICM + TUV-x + offline emissions only (anthropogenic, prescribed biogenic, prescribed fires). Target: August 2026.

2. **MIEM's role:** MIEM is the C++ implementation of what the design exploration called `chempas_emissions_offline` -- the offline emission reader module. The design originally specified Fortran source modules (`chempas_emis_state.F90`, `chempas_emissions_offline.F90`, `chempas_emis_species_map.F90`), but MIEM implements this as C++ core with Fortran bindings via the MUSICA three-layer pattern (C++ -> C API -> Fortran `iso_c_binding`).

3. **Three architectural seams:**
   - **Seam 1 (Host/Chemistry):** Typed state objects (EmisState, ChemState, MetState) as the data contract between MPAS pools and the chemistry layer
   - **Seam 2 (Chemistry/Processes):** Abstract process interface with init/run/finalize lifecycle
   - **Seam 3 (CheMPAS-A/MUSICA):** Unit conversion (kg/kg to mol/m3), precision promotion (single to double), copy-in/copy-out

4. **Process ordering constraint:** Emissions MUST execute before chemistry. The pipeline is: `emissions_offline -> photolysis (TUV-x) -> gas_chemistry (MICM)`.

5. **Risk R9 was prescient:** "Emission pipeline complexity underestimated" -- all five design agents flagged emissions as under-specified and needing dedicated design attention. MIEM is the response to that risk.

6. **10 design gaps resolved:** Including file format spec (CF-compliant NetCDF3, `(Time, nCells)`, `emi_<SPECIES>` naming, `kg m-2 s-1`), temporal interpolation (linear for monthly, step for daily/hourly), vertical distribution (surface-only for v1), and non-1:1 species mapping (VOC speciation via multi-target mapping with scaling factors).

The `emissions-extraction` branch of the design repo contains the complete consolidated context, including Fortran prototypes and test specifications (10 files total) that informed MIEM's C++ implementation.

---

**Sources:**

- [PACE-DAAQ/MPAS-GOCART2G](https://github.com/PACE-DAAQ/MPAS-GOCART2G) -- MPAS-GOCART2G source code
- [PACE-DAAQ/UPTEMPO](https://github.com/PACE-DAAQ/UPTEMPO) -- Unified Processing Tool for Emissions in MPAS-A GOCART
- [NCAR/chempas-emissions-design](https://github.com/NCAR/chempas-emissions-design) -- CheMPAS-A v1 emissions architecture
- [NCAR/micm](https://github.com/NCAR/micm) -- Model Independent Chemistry Module
- [NCAR/musica](https://github.com/NCAR/musica) -- Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry Modeling
- [ESCOMP/HEMCO_CESM](https://github.com/ESCOMP/HEMCO_CESM) -- HEMCO integration in CESM
- [HEMCO in CAM PR #560](https://github.com/ESCOMP/CAM/pull/560) -- CAM HEMCO integration pull request
- [CAM-SIMA Chemistry](https://sima.ucar.edu/applications/v0/chemistry) -- MUSICA v0 chemistry documentation
- [HEMCO 3.0 paper (Lin et al., 2021 GMD)](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/14/5487/2021/) -- HEMCO reference publication

This paints a much clearer picture. Here's the synthesis:

## Why UPTEMPO exists (and why the host model doesn't just regrid)

UPTEMPO exists because **MPAS can't do mass-conservative regridding at runtime**. MPAS's native interpolation is bilinear (fine for meteorology), but emissions require conservative remapping to avoid creating or destroying mass. ESMF conservative regridding needs precomputed weight files between source and target grids, and computing those weights for a 0.1° global inventory onto an unstructured Voronoi mesh is expensive. UPTEMPO computes them once per grid pair and reuses them.

But this is an **MPAS-specific limitation**, not a universal one. CAM-SIMA with HEMCO already does runtime ESMF regridding — it reads native-grid inventories and regrids on the fly. The community is moving in that direction.

## What MIEM actually replaces in GOCART-2G

MIEM replaces the **entire offline emissions reading/processing pipeline**:

| GOCART-2G component | MIEM replacement |
|---|---|
| `emis_gocart2G` type (60+ hardcoded pointer arrays) | `EmisState` with runtime-configured species |
| Per-species `init_anth_emissions_*` subroutines | `OfflineEmissionSource::Update()` |
| `Registry_gocart2G_emissions.xml` (50+ compile-time vars) | YAML configuration |
| Hardcoded VOC speciation factors | `SpeciesMap` with YAML scaling |
| `FluxToMixingRatio` in `GOCART2G_Process.F90` | `FluxConverter::Convert()` |

MIEM does **not** replace: online emissions (dust, sea-salt, DMS), GOCART-2G aerosol chemistry, or the MPAS↔GOCART grid interface layer.

## How MIEM feeds into MICM

The chain is:
1. **`QuerySpecies()`** — host discovers what species MIEM will produce
2. **`ResolveHostIndices(host_species)`** — maps MIEM species to the host's tracer array (which comes from MICM's mechanism config)
3. **`Run()`** — produces `EmisState` with tendencies in kg/kg/s
4. **Host adds tendencies to chemistry state** — `tendency * dt` added to species concentrations before calling `MICM::Solve()` (Lie operator splitting: emissions before chemistry)

There's no direct MIEM→MICM coupling. The host mediates.

## What this means for the grid/convention question

The key insight: **the regridding question is really about where MIEM sits in the pipeline**.

- If MIEM reads **pre-regridded files** → UPTEMPO (or equivalent) is required per model, but MIEM is simple
- If MIEM reads **native-grid files** → the host's ESMF infrastructure regrids at runtime, UPTEMPO is unnecessary, but MIEM must handle 2D spatial layouts
- CAM-SIMA/HEMCO already demonstrates the runtime-regridding approach works

The CheMPAS design docs themselves note that HEMCO's MPAS compatibility was flagged as needing evaluation, with the fallback being "modernize UPTEMPO."

options.label: Native grids (lat/lon)
options.description: MIEM reads native-grid emissions and exposes 2D arrays. The host model regrids using its own ESMF infrastructure. One input file serves all models. UPTEMPO becomes unnecessary for basic regridding. Convention defines lat/lon layout.

options.label: Pre-regridded only (current)
options.description: Keep nCells. Each host model needs its own preprocessing tool (UPTEMPO for MPAS, SE tools for CAM). MIEM stays simple but input files are grid-specific.

options.label: Both (phased)
options.description: v1: support native lat/lon grids as the primary path. Also support pre-regridded 1D via DatasetDescriptor for models that prefer offline regridding. Convention defines both layouts.

options.label: Optional sectors (v1)

options.label: No sectors (current)
options.description: Keep simple. Host can use multiple source configs as pseudo-sectors. Loses runtime sector diagnostics and scenario perturbation.

options.label: First-class sectors
options.description: HEMCO-style category/hierarchy with sector-specific temporal profiles and scale factors. Powerful but significantly more complex for v1.

questions.question: NetCDF-4 + CF Conventions for the input format? (Research confirmed: every inventory is NetCDF, Fortran interop is trivial, HPC availability is universal, dimension semantics match emissions data. Parquet has no Fortran bindings.)

options.label: NetCDF-4 confirmed
options.description: Stay with NetCDF-4 + CF Conventions. Consider Parquet only for the separate preprocessing tool's internal pipeline.

options.label: Explore further
options.description: Want to investigate alternatives more before committing.

questions.question: Convention name — given that the convention standardizes dimensions, naming, units, and metadata for emissions (and possibly defines both native and preprocessed grid layouts)?

options.label: Standardized Emissions Schema
options.description: SES — describes what it does: standardizes structure. Stays accurate regardless of grid strategy or sector support. 'Schema' = structural convention, not a rigid format.

options.label: Compact Emissions Schema
options.description: CES — keeps existing abbreviation. 'Compact' is only accurate if data is being compressed/aggregated during preprocessing.

options.label: Model-Ready Emissions
options.description: MRE — descriptive, community-familiar. But vague and doesn't convey what the convention structurally specifies.

input.prompt:
Research the MUSICA (Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols) architecture and how it relates to MIEM, MICM, TUV-x, and online emissions. Specifically:

1. **MUSICA's role as an integrator**: What is MUSICA exactly — is it a framework, a library, a coupler? How does it compose MICM, TUV-x, and emissions modules? What is the `musica` C++ library on GitHub (NCAR/musica)?

2. **How MUSICA wraps science modules**: Does MUSICA provide a common interface that MICM, TUV-x, and MIEM all implement? Or is each module independently integrated into host models?

3. **MUSICA and host model coupling**: How does MUSICA connect to MPAS-A and CAM-SIMA? Is there a MUSICA runtime that orchestrates the modules, or does the host model call each module individually?

4. **Online emissions in GOCART-2G and beyond**: What are the online emissions in GOCART-2G (dust, sea-salt, DMS, volcanic, biogenic via MEGAN)? How are they parameterized — do they depend on meteorological state (wind speed, soil moisture, SST, LAI)? Could these eventually be handled by the same module that handles offline emissions, or are they fundamentally different?

5. **GOCART-3G**: Is there a GOCART-3G design or plan? What would it look like? If MIEM is meant to represent "all GOCART-3G emissions logic," what does that scope include beyond what MIEM currently does?

6. **The EmissionSource abstraction in MIEM**: MIEM already has an abstract `EmissionSource` base class with `OfflineEmissionSource` as the concrete implementation. The design docs mention extensibility for dust, sea-salt, biogenic. How would online sources fit into this architecture?

7. **What online emissions need that offline don't**: Online emissions typically need meteorological state (wind speed for dust/sea-salt, temperature/PAR for biogenic MEGAN, SST for DMS). How would MIEM receive this state — same pattern as air_density/layer_thickness, or something different?

Search GitHub (NCAR/musica, NCAR/micm, NCAR/tuv-x, NCAR/chempas-emissions-design, PACE-DAAQ/MPAS-GOCART2G), web documentation, and any MUSICA papers/presentations.

This is pure research — do not modify any files.

Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols

MUSICA is a collection of modeling software, tools, and grids, that
allow for robust modeling of chemistry in Earth's atmosphere.

At present the project encompasses these core components
- [TUV-x](https://github.com/NCAR/tuv-x)
    - A photolysis rate calculator 

- [MICM](https://github.com/NCAR/micm)
    - Model Independent Chemical Module

- [CARMA](https://github.com/ESCOMP/CARMA)
    - Community Aerosol and Radiation Model for Atmospheres (integration in development)

- [Mechanism Configuration](https://github.com/NCAR/MechanismConfiguration)
    - The standardized format to describe atmospheric chemistry

These components are used to drive the MUSICA software ecosystem. This is a snapshot of how MUSICA can be used with different
models.

![MUSICA Ecosystem](docs/source/_static/ecosystem.png)

# Installation

MUSICA provides interfaces for multiple programming languages. Choose the installation method that best fits your needs:

## Python

Most scientific users may prefer our python interface. It can be installed with pip:

```bash
pip install musica
```

For detailed Python installation instructions, usage examples, and development information, see the [Python README](python/README.md).

## JavaScript

The JavaScript interface uses WebAssembly to run MUSICA components. This interface is most for tools developed for web 
browsers and only supports the C++ components of MUSICA. It can be installed from npm

```bash
npm install @ncar/musica
```

For detailed JavaScript installation instructions, usage examples, and development information, see the [JavaScript README](javascript/README.md).

## Fortran

The Fortran interface is designed for integration with Fortran-based atmospheric models. You can install this from spack

```bash
spack install musica
```

For detailed Fortran installation instructions, usage examples, and development information, see the [Fortran README](fortran/README.md).

## C++ / CMake

For C++ development or building from source with full control over options:

### Prerequisites

Minimum required packages:
- cmake (>= 3.21)
- pkg-config
- netcdf
- netcdf-fortran
- blas
- lapack

### Building from Source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NCAR/musica.git
cd musica
mkdir build
cd build
ccmake ..
make
make install
```

## GOCART-2G Overview

The Goddard Chemistry Aerosol Radiation and Transport (GOCART) model simulates major tropospheric aerosol components, including sulfate, dust, black carbon (BC), organic carbon (OC), and sea-salt aerosols.

## Online Emissions Capabilities

Due to the mechanism for biogenic emissions introduced in GOCART-2G, there is an increase in the total emissions of organic matter relative to legacy GOCART. This indicates that GOCART-2G includes an improved online biogenic emissions mechanism.

## Specific Parameterizations

**DMS Emissions:** Oceanic emission of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) is calculated based on the surface seawater concentrations of DMS and 10-m winds over the ocean using an empirical formula (Liss and Merlivat, 1986).

**Dust Emissions:** Dust emissions follow Ginoux et al. (2001), see Table 1.

**Sea Salt:** Addition of a correction term dependent on sea surface temperature, similar to the work of Jaegle et al. (2011) but tuned to improve the agreement of simulated sea salt AOD with MODIS retrieved AOD.

**Biogenic Emissions:** Biogenic emissions are calculated by WRF-CHIMERE using the MEGAN model, (Model of Emissions of Gases and Aerosols from Nature). MEGAN provides the parameterization for online biogenic emissions in WRF systems that use GOCART aerosols.

# CheMPAS-A Design Exploration

Multi-agent design exploration and v1 emissions architecture for the Chemistry in MPAS (CheMPAS-A) project.

## Branch Guide

| Branch | Contents |
|--------|----------|
| `main` | Design exploration output only (Phase 1-3 documents + synthesis) |
| `emissions-extraction` | Everything on `main` + consolidated emissions extraction + v1 implementation (Fortran, configs, tests, design decisions) |

## Directory Structure

```
├── design-exploration-output/    # Multi-agent design exploration documents
│   ├── synthesis.md              #   Final synthesis (14 consensus decisions, 13 risks)
│   ├── emissions-extraction.md   #   Emissions-specific extraction from all phases
│   ├── phase1-*.md               #   5 independent agent perspectives
│   ├── phase2_*.md               #   4 cross-pollinated analyses
│   └── phase3_devils_advocate.md #   Devil's advocate challenge document
│
├── emissions-design_exploration/ # v1 emissions implementation
│   ├── src/                      #   Fortran source modules
│   ├── tests/                    #   Unit and integration tests
│   ├── config/                   #   YAML configuration examples
│   ├── docs/                     #   Design decisions document
│   └── emissions-extraction.md   #   Single source of truth for implementation
│
└── consolidated_context/         # Pre-processed markdown summaries (agent input)
```

## Emissions v1 Deliverables

| # | File | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | `src/chempas_emis_state.F90` | EmisState type — flat v1 stub holding external emission fields |
| 2 | `src/chempas_emissions_offline.F90` | Offline emission reader: NetCDF I/O, temporal interpolation, species mapping, flux-to-tendency conversion |
| 3 | `src/chempas_emis_species_map.F90` | Species mapping: YAML parse, inventory-to-mechanism mapping with scaling factors, validation |
| 4 | `config/emissions.yaml` | Example emissions config (sectors, file paths, update frequencies) |
| 5 | `config/species_mapping.yaml` | Example species mapping (CAMS inventory to MICM mechanism species) |
| 6 | `tests/test_emissions_flux_to_tendency.F90` | Flux (kg/m2/s) to tendency (kg/kg/s) conversion, <1e-12 relative error |
| 7 | `tests/test_emissions_species_mapping.F90` | YAML mapping resolution, unmapped species warning |
| 8 | `tests/test_emissions_mass_conservation.F90` | Emission mass = flux x area x dt, <1e-12 relative error |
| 9 | `tests/test_emissions_non_negativity.F90` | Negative flux triggers error at read time |
| 10 | `docs/design-decisions.md` | Resolution of all 10 design gaps (see below) |

## Design Gaps Resolved

The design exploration identified 10 open questions for emissions. All are resolved in `docs/design-decisions.md`:

1. **File format spec** — CF-compliant NetCDF3, `(Time, nCells)` layout, `emi_<SPECIES>` naming, `kg m-2 s-1`
2. **Temporal interpolation** — Linear for monthly, step for daily/hourly, configurable per sector
3. **Vertical distribution** — Surface-only injection for v1 (lowest model layer)
4. **Non-1:1 species mapping** — VOC speciation via multi-target mapping with scaling factors
5. **EmisState design** — Flat structure for v1 (no sector hierarchy until v2)
6. **HEMCO evaluation** — Assessment of HEMCO on MPAS unstructured grids (evaluation only)
7. **UPTEMPO modernization** — Changes needed for 128+ tracer support
8. **Pseudocode for emissions_offline** — Full read-interpolate-map-inject pipeline
9. **Sector update frequencies** — Generalized time-tracker pattern (monthly/daily/hourly)
10. **Error handling** — Missing emission files trigger warnings, missing mapped species trigger errors

## How It Was Built

This implementation was produced through a three-stage process:

1. **Design exploration** — 5 AI agents (Technical Architect, Engineering Lead, Scientific Lead, Cutting Edge, Devil's Advocate) independently analyzed the CheMPAS-A problem space, then cross-pollinated and debated to produce a synthesis with 14 consensus decisions.

2. **Emissions extraction** — All emissions-relevant decisions were consolidated from the 11 exploration documents into a single reference (`emissions-extraction.md`).

3. **Implementation** — A 3-agent team (Engineer, Scientist, Reviewer) implemented the v1 architecture from the extraction document, resolving all 10 design gaps along the way.

## v1 Scope

**Included (offline emissions):**
- Anthropogenic emissions (CAMS inventory via UPTEMPO)
- Prescribed biogenic emissions (pre-calculated files)
- Prescribed fire emissions (FINN v2.5 via UPTEMPO)

**Deferred to v2/v3:**
- Online dust (Ginoux/Kok schemes)
- Online sea-salt (Gong scheme)
- Online biogenic (MEGAN)
- Fire plume rise (Freitas)
- Lightning NOx
- Ocean/DMS (OASISS)

## 1. Project Motivation

### WRF-Chem Legacy

The Weather Research and Forecasting model with Chemistry (WRF-Chem) is a widely utilized and actively co-developed community model (Grell et al., 2005; Powers et al., 2017) that couples meteorological processes with atmospheric chemistry. Its impact is documented by **2705 publications** sourced from the OpenAlex catalog (Priem et al., 2022), spanning topics including:

- Air quality analysis across regions (Chouza et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023)
- Health and environmental impact assessments (Ghude et al., 2016; Young et al., 2018)
- Field campaign forecasting and analysis (Kumar et al., 2019; Pfister et al., 2019)

- Chemistry-weather interactions (Fast et al., 2006; Pickering et al., 2024)
- Downscaling global chemistry-climate models (Pfister et al., 2014; Yahya et al., 2017)
- Compatibility with DART data assimilation (Anderson et al., 2009)
- Large Eddy Simulation (LES) capability (Moeng et al., 1984)

Highly cited WRF-Chem research covers aerosol-climate interactions, biomass burning, mineral dust, ozone, urban emissions, and data assimilation.

    26→
    27→### Why a New Architecture Is Needed (Not Just Porting)
    28→
    29→Current global and regional chemical transport models inadequately account for the **two-way coupling** of atmospheric chemistry with other Earth system components over the range of urban/local to regional to global scales and from the surface to the top of the atmosphere. The community is moving toward unified modeling frameworks (Pfister et al., 2020). New "stretch grid" mesh structures enable simulations that resolve urban emissions at exposure-relevant resolutions while simultaneously capturing global teleconnections (e.g., ENSO) within a physically and chemically consistent multi-scale framework.
    30→
    31→NSF NCAR is replacing WRF and WRF-Chem with new initiatives including **MPAS-A** (Snider et al., 2024) and **SIMA** (System for Integrated Modeling of the Atmosphere). However:
    32→
    33→- **MPAS-A does not include chemistry**
    34→- **SIMA** (based on CESM, Danabasoglu et al., 2020) does not yet offer limited-area capability or LES modeling, and likely will not for several years
    35→
    36→A **direct port of WRF-Chem's capabilities into MPAS-A would bring along all of its technical debt**, leading to:
    37→- Loss of clarity
    38→- Prohibitive maintenance and development costs
    39→- Negative impact on research
    40→
    41→The WRF-Chem codebase suffered from "historical accretion of code" as more elaborate chemistry and physics parameterizations were introduced, resulting in complexity that:
    42→- Led to prohibitive maintenance costs
    43→- Increased the risk of introducing bugs
    44→- Degraded the user experience
    45→
    46→The proposal states: "Porting the existing capabilities of WRF-Chem in their current form would simply recreate these limitations in MPAS-A." Innovation and the adoption of tools and techniques from other fields are required instead.
    47→
    48→### Current State of Atmospheric Chemistry Modeling
    49→
    50→- The U.S. EPA has switched from WRF to MPAS-A for their Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model, developing MPAS-CMAQ (Wong et al., 2024)
    51→- MPAS-CMAQ has limited modularity and flexibility, posing a hurdle for community contributions of new parameterizations
    52→- MPAS-CMAQ is focused on air quality and does not cover the full breadth of atmospheric sciences research needs
    53→- Some NSF NCAR team members have been funded by NASA (Grant #80NSSC24K1786) to implement GOCART-2G aerosols in MPAS-A, expected available summer 2025
    54→

    57→## 2. MPAS-A Capabilities
    58→
    59→### Core Architecture
    60→
    61→- **MPAS** (Model for Prediction Across Scales) began in the early 2010s as a collaborative project between NSF NCAR and DOE Los Alamos National Laboratory
    62→- NSF NCAR focuses on the atmosphere component: **MPAS-A**
    63→- The dynamical core is well-suited for simulating the atmosphere at **convection-resolving scales**
    64→
    65→### Voronoi Tessellation Mesh
    66→
    67→- Horizontal meshes are **centroidal Voronoi tessellations**, enabling smooth refinement of grid resolution down to **kilometer and smaller scales**
    68→- Both **global and limited-area domains** are supported
    69→- Permits applications from global seasonal to sub-seasonal prediction to regional, high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP)
    70→- The "stretch grid" mesh structures enable simulations that resolve urban emissions at exposure-relevant resolutions while capturing global teleconnections (e.g., ENSO)
    71→
    72→### GPU Port Plans
    73→
    74→- The current release (v8.2.2) supports a **limited capability to run on GPUs**
    75→- Ongoing work to port the entire model to GPUs using a **directive-based approach**
    76→- Plans for a GPU port could significantly accelerate a chemistry capability
    77→
    78→### JEDI/DART Data Assimilation
    79→
    80→- An interface to **JEDI** (Joint Effort for Data Assimilation Integration) has been developed for MPAS-A to support assimilation of polar orbiting and geostationary atmospheric composition satellite data (Guerrette et al., 2023; Ha et al., 2024)
    81→- MPAS-A can also be used with the **Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART)** (Ha et al., 2017)
    82→
    83→### LES Support
    84→
    85→- MPAS-A supports Large Eddy Simulations, a capability inherited from WRF physics parameterizations
    86→- SIMA does not yet offer LES modeling capability
    87→
    88→### Scalability
    89→
    90→- Supports execution on parallel computing clusters through domain decomposition with both **MPI and OpenMP**
    91→- Scalability demonstrated to over **400,000 processor cores** (Heinzeller et al., 2016)
    92→

    94→
    95→- MPAS-A uses physical parameterization schemes from WRF, well tested in short-term prediction and NWP
    96→- MPAS-A's dynamical core has been implemented in CESM CAM, with efforts underway to implement it in CAM-SIMA and NOAA's Unified Forecasting System (UFS)
    97→- MPAS-A is well-suited for urban applications

   222→## 4. Phases A/B/C Detail (from ABR Q&A doc)
   223→
   224→The ABR (Annual Budget Review) document defines three development phases that represent the current operative planning framework:
   225→
   226→### Phase A: CheMPAS-A Minimum Viable Version (Gas Phase Chemistry and Offline Emissions)
   227→
   228→**Funded by:** NSF CSSI QUACS project
   229→
   230→- CheMPAS-A has **runtime configuration capabilities** for MUSICA constituents and processes.
   231→- An **interface between MPAS-A and the MUSICA library** is created, containing MICM (gas chemistry kinetics and solver) and TUV-x (photolysis rates).
   232→- MICM is expected to have a **multiphase chemistry solver** implemented as part of another project. CheMPAS-A will need to provide additional information (e.g., liquid water content) from MPAS-A to the MUSICA library for the multiphase solver.
   233→- CheMPAS-A reads **offline anthropogenic, biogenic, and fire emissions** from gridded datasets.
   234→
   235→**Key rationale for CSSI scope limitation:** The CSSI program targets cyberinfrastructure challenges. Implementing chemistry and aerosols in MPAS-A is not considered a cyberinfrastructure challenge; only the scripting interface (QUACS) qualifies. Therefore, only a small part of model development work could be included in the CSSI proposal.

   237→### Phase B: CheMPAS-A Basic Version (GOCART-2G Aerosols and Deposition)

   239→**Funded by:** ABR/CSF request

   241→- CheMPAS-A represents **aerosol physics** by updating the GOCART-2G configuration of MPAS-A and connecting it with the MUSICA library.

   250→# Requirements and Specifications
   251→
   252→> **Sources:** MPAS-A-Chem_Requirements.docx, Concept of Operations_UFS-Chem_Final.docx, Structure of UFS-Chem.docx, Target Parameterizations_.pptx, Development Task Templates/, Working Groups.docx
   253→> **Purpose:** What CheMPAS-A must do -- process requirements, architecture specs, UFS-Chem reference design, development task breakdown.

   257→
   258→## 1. Process Ordering
   259→
   260→The process ordering is derived from the WRF-Chem driver (`chem/chem_driver.F`) and is intended to be preserved at least initially:
   261→
   262→1. **Initialization of meteorology variables** as needed for chemistry
   263→2. **emissions_driver** -- inject emissions into the chemistry state
   264→3. **photolysis_driver** -- compute photolysis rate constants
   265→4. **dry_dep_driver** -- calculate dry deposition velocities and fluxes
   266→5. **uoc_dustwd_driver** -- dust wet deposition (specific dust/ocean processes)
   267→6. **grelldrvct** -- convective tracer transport
   268→7. **mechanism_driver** -- gas-phase chemistry (chemical kinetics solver)
   269→8. **cloud_chem_driver** -- aqueous/cloud chemistry
   270→9. **aerosols_driver** -- aerosol processes (nucleation, coagulation, condensation, optical properties)
   271→10. **wetscav_driver** -- wet scavenging (both resolved and convective)
   272→11. **sum_pm_driver** -- summation of particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10)
   273→
   274→### Rationale
   275→
   276→- This ordering was proven effective in WRF-Chem over many years of operational and research use.
   277→- Emissions are injected first so that freshly emitted species are available to all subsequent chemistry and removal processes within the same timestep.
   278→- Photolysis precedes the gas-phase mechanism because photolysis rate constants are needed by the chemical kinetics solver.
   279→- Dry deposition is computed before gas-phase chemistry to allow removal to be factored into the chemical state.
   280→- Convective transport occurs before the mechanism driver so that transport-modified concentrations feed into chemistry.
   281→- Aerosol processes follow gas-phase chemistry because many aerosol precursors are produced by gas-phase reactions.
   282→- Wet scavenging follows aerosol calculations so that the latest aerosol size/composition information is available.
   283→- PM summation occurs last as a diagnostic aggregation step.
   284→
   285→### Flexibility / Configurability
   286→
   287→- The MPAS-A-Chem requirements document explicitly notes: "Over time making this order of processes more flexible would be useful."
   288→- The Concept of Operations states: "Processes will be allowed to be called in different orders to facilitate complicated interactions between chemistry and physics (e.g., photolysis including aerosol feedbacks, convective transport and convective wet scavenging, PBL mixing, and aqueous chemistry)."
   289→- The system is not required to use "drivers" for these tasks; the team may adopt a more modern architecture. The driver structure is primarily a reference for which processes to consider and their default sequence.
   290→- The UFS-Chem architecture requires that these complicated interactions be "written in a generalized way such that no chemistry information is hard-wired in the code."
   291→
   292→---
   293→
   294→## 2. Chemical Mechanisms Catalog
   295→
   296→All mechanisms are intended to be incorporated through MICM (Model Independent Chemistry Module), part of the MUSICA library, enabling runtime configurability. Users can also choose to include no gas-phase chemistry.
   297→
   298→### 2.1 GHG (Greenhouse Gas)
   299→
   300→- **Scope:** Simplest gas-phase chemistry -- greenhouse gas tracers (CO2, CH4, SF6) with offline prescribed oxidants.
   301→- **Application:** Long-duration runs for data assimilation of long-lived GHG species.
   302→- **Key feature:** Minimizes unnecessary computation; flexible tracer addition/editing of chemical properties.
   303→- **Mass conservation:** Monitoring and prioritization for all processes.
   304→
   305→### 2.2 AM4 (GFDL Atmosphere Model v4.1)
   306→
   307→- **Scope:** Full stratospheric chemistry (O3, HOy, NOy, Cly, Bry, polar clouds) and tropospheric chemistry (O3, CO, CH4, NOx, VOCs, SO2, DMS). Includes simple SOA scheme.
   308→- **Application:** Initial gas-phase chemistry in CATChem; global applications.
   309→- **Tracers:** 128 total (87 prognostic, 41 diagnostic, 21 aerosols).
   310→- **Reactions:** 248 (43 photolysis, 205 kinetic).
   311→- **Note:** AM4 stratospheric chemistry will serve as the default stratospheric extension for tropospheric-only mechanisms (CRACMM, RACM-ESRL-VCP, RACM2B-VCP).
   312→
   313→### 2.3 REDHC (Reduced Hydrocarbon)
   314→
   315→- **Scope:** Simplified carbon-bond scheme based on Houweling et al. (1998); accurately represents ozone and PM2.5 for regional forecasting with limited computational cost.
   316→- **Application:** Large domains, high resolution, long time periods, or data assimilation runs where computational cost is the binding constraint.
   317→- **Origin:** Currently used in the experimental RAP-Chem model (Benjamin et al., 2016).
   318→
   319→### 2.4 RACM-ESRL-VCP
   320→
   321→- **Scope:** Builds from RACM-ESRL (Stockwell et al., 1997; Geiger et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2009) with added VCP (volatile chemical product) chemistry (Coggon et al., 2021). Uses VBS (volatility basis set) for SOA (Ahmadov et al., 2012).
   322→- **Application:** Moderately complex; suitable for source apportionment but still computationally efficient. Used in FIM-Chem for global chemical weather forecasts (Zhang et al., 2022b).
   323→
   324→### 2.5 CRACMM (Community Regional Atmospheric Chemistry Multiphase Mechanism)
   325→
   326→- **Scope:** Advanced mechanism for ozone, particulate matter, and air toxics. Fully connects SOA formation with gas-phase chemistry producing ozone and air toxics. Supported by EPA.
   327→- **Application:** Source apportionment applications; regional air quality. More complex than RACM-ESRL-VCP.
   328→- **Code repository:** https://github.com/USEPA/CRACMM (directly linked to CATChem).
   329→- **Key feature:** Unlike traditional mechanisms, CRACMM fully couples SOA formation with gas-phase chemistry.
   330→
   331→### 2.6 RACM2B-VCP
   332→
   333→- **Scope:** Most complex mechanism. Builds from RACM2-Berkeley2.0 with updates to ketones, aromatics, biogenics (Goliff et al., 2013), isoprene and monoterpenes (Browne et al., 2014; Zare et al., 2018), plus VCP additions.
   334→- **Application:** Field campaign analysis where direct comparison of chemical species to observations is needed. More complex than CRACMM for some chemical systems. Not prohibitive for short-duration field campaign simulations.
   335→- **SOA:** Similar approach to RACM-ESRL-VCP.
   336→
   337→### 2.7 RAQMS (Real-time Air Quality Modeling System)
   338→
   339→- **Scope:** Simplified tropospheric and stratospheric chemistry for ozone and aerosols (Pierce et al., 2003, 2007, 2021).
   340→- **Application:** Global forecasting. Low computational cost.
   341→- **Note:** In UFS-Chem, RAQMS gas-phase chemistry is implemented through MICM and users can optionally connect any aerosol scheme.
   342→
   343→### Mechanism Selection and Configuration
   344→
   345→- Mechanisms are selected via YAML/JSON configuration files -- no recompilation needed.
   346→- MICM preprocesses the chemical reactions and solves the ODEs.
   347→- Each mechanism includes mapping files for: species parameters, deposition, SOA, emissions, photolysis, and initial/boundary conditions.
   348→- Gas-phase components of SOA and POA are included in the gas-phase chemistry scheme to encourage full coupling.
   349→- Future possibility: Users could select complexity per chemical system (e.g., simplified isoprene vs. nearly explicit).
   350→
   351→---
   352→
   353→## 3. Aerosol Packages
   354→
   355→Aerosol packages can be linked to any gas-phase mechanism. Users can also choose no aerosols.
   356→
   357→### 3.1 Smoke/Dust (SD)
   358→
   359→- **Scope:** Simplest aerosol scheme -- tracers for smoke and dust only.
   360→- **Application:** Smoke and dust forecasting (as in RRFS-SD).
   361→
   362→### 3.2 NASA GOCART (2nd Generation)
   363→
   364→- **Scope:** Bulk aerosol model -- black carbon, organic carbon, sulfate, dust, sea salt with prescribed oxidant fields. Latest version adds ammonium, nitrates, and brown carbon (Collow et al., in review).
   365→- **Application:** Simple, low computational cost; global weather forecasts with aerosol feedbacks.
   366→- **Code:** https://github.com/GEOS-ESM/GOCART
   367→- **Coupling:** Connected through CCPP at the process level (not as a wrapper), allowing users to swap individual processes.
   368→- **Tracers:** 20 (all prognostic: 3 gases, 17 aerosols).
   369→- **Reactions:** 3 (simple sulfur chemistry with prescribed oxidants).
